title: Gemini South Reveals Tangled Spiral Arms of the Peculiar Galaxy NGC 7727
caption: The peculiar galaxy NGC 7727, imaged by the Gemini South telescope
celestial: NGC 7727 · constellation Aquarius · about 73 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Official NSF NOIRLab / Gemini press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: Tangled spiral arms twist around the peculiar galaxy NGC 7727 in this Gemini South image. The scene is the aftermath, some billion years on, of a collision between two spiral galaxies, and it lies about 73 million light-years away in the direction of Aquarius.

Entwined at the center of the merger is a pair of supermassive black holes, described as the closest such pair ever recorded from Earth. Large galaxies are generally thought to host a supermassive black hole at their centers, so when two galaxies merge, their central black holes can end up close together.

Over very long times, such a pair is expected to draw closer still. Gemini South, which forms half of the International Gemini Observatory run by NSF NOIRLab, recorded NGC 7727 with the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph through g, r, i and hydrogen-alpha filters, revealing the disturbed structure left behind by the collision.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (5.31 x 5.14 arcminutes) and distance (73 million light years), the frame spans roughly 113,000 × 109,000 light-years. Its light set out about 73 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Taken in visible light with the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph on Gemini South through g, r, i and hydrogen-alpha filters. The color mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The long exposure gathers far more light than the eye, bringing out faint, tangled arms around the galaxy.
